study.title: A black hole star at cosmic dawn: MoM-BH*-1 and the nature of little red dots

cover.headline: The early universe might never have broken its own timeline. **We were reading the light wrong.**

slides.title: If the little red dots are all built like this one, the early universe stops looking impossible.
slides.body:
Read as dusty galaxies, the dots need more stars forming faster than there was time to build them. That is the crisis.

Read as gas-wrapped black holes, the crisis may simply go away. One object cannot settle it.

slides.title: The reddening is not dust. It is a cocoon of hydrogen gas wrapped around a black hole.
slides.body:
At specific wavelengths the light simply vanished, which dense hydrogen does and dust does not.

The best fit inside the cocoon is a black hole feeding hard, buried in gas thick enough that the whole object mimics one enormous star.

stat.label: years after the Big Bang, this existed

slides.title: JWST kept finding tiny red dots in the early universe that nobody could explain.
slides.body:
Since Webb switched on, its deep images have been littered with compact, very red points of light from the first billion years.

The obvious reading was dust, which reddens light the way smoke reddens a sunset.

caveats: This is one object. A category of cosmic thing does not get established on a single example.
The interpretation leans on model fitting, so a different model could still fit the same light.
Mass estimates for objects this far away carry wide error bars that headlines tend to drop.

caption: The most annoying objects in astronomy might not be impossible galaxies. They might be black holes wearing a gas coat.
